html:
The map's label for the farming peoples of New Guinea and nearby islands, shown from 1500 to 400 BCE. New Guinea is one of the few places in the world where people invented farming on their own.

At Kuk Swamp in the highlands, people dug drains and planted gardens between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago. They grew taro, bananas and yams, and New Guinea is where sugarcane was first tamed. Farming let highland valleys hold dense populations.

The peoples spoke many different Papuan languages, which do not form one family. From about 1500 BCE Austronesian newcomers, the Lapita, settled the coasts and offshore islands and traded pottery and obsidian with them. Their later history continues under Papuans.
